blocks.text: You have learned an enormous amount of pandas across the earlier modules in this course, filtering, grouping, merging, cleaning, feature engineering, all of it. This new module is about a different kind of skill: making all of that genuinely fast once your data actually gets big. This first lesson starts with the single most important performance habit in all of pandas, thinking in vectorized operations instead of row by row loops.

blocks.caption: The exact same reason NumPy is fast is the reason a vectorized pandas Series operation is fast too.

blocks.text: Back in the NumPy Fundamentals module you learned why vectorization is fast, a vectorized call runs in compiled C code instead of paying Python's per iteration overhead for every single element. A pandas Series is literally backed by a NumPy array, so every reason NumPy vectorization is fast applies directly to pandas too. This lesson does not re-explain that mechanism. It applies it specifically to the everyday pandas patterns people reach for out of habit, and shows the genuinely vectorized alternative for each one.

You also already know from the Apply lesson that .apply() still secretly loops in Python under the hood, which is why it is usually slower than it looks. This lesson goes one level further, past just avoiding apply, into the specific pandas tools that replace it entirely.
A huge share of row wise apply calls exist purely to implement simple if/else logic. np.where() does exactly that, fully vectorized, with no loop at all.

blocks.caption: One line, no loop, the entire column decided in a single vectorized pass.

blocks.text: np.where only handles two outcomes. When you have several conditions, the kind of logic you would normally write as if/elif/elif/else inside an apply call, np.select() handles all of those branches at once, still fully vectorized.

code.content:
conditions = [
    df["score"] >= 90,
    df["score"] >= 70,
    df["score"] >= 50,
]
choices = ["A", "B", "C"]
df["grade"] = np.select(conditions, choices, default="F")

blocks.caption: This replaces an entire if/elif chain inside an apply call with one vectorized call.

blocks.title: pd.cut and pd.qcut are also vectorized binning tools
blocks.content: You already covered pd.cut() and pd.qcut() in the Feature Creation lesson. Worth remembering here specifically as a performance point: they are vectorized alternatives to writing your own manual binning function inside an apply call.

blocks.text: You already learned the .str accessor in the String Operations lesson. Worth calling out explicitly here: every .str method is already fully vectorized. There is never a reason to loop over a text column calling a plain Python string method row by row when .str already does the same thing at full speed.

blocks.caption: This is the same general performance principle you already know from string operations, just named explicitly here.

blocks.text: 5. Vectorized Boolean Logic on Full Columns

This is a genuinely common performance mistake that beginners make without realizing a fully vectorized equivalent already exists. Combining multiple conditions with & and | directly on whole columns is completely vectorized. Writing a custom function that compares values one row at a time and passing it to apply is not, even though it produces the same result.

blocks.alt: Vectorized Boolean Logic on Full Columns
blocks.caption: You already write this correctly from the Filtering lesson. This is the exact same pattern, just named as a performance win here.

code.content:
# fully vectorized, fast
mask = (df["price"] > 100) & (df["region"] == "west")

# do not do this instead
def check(row):
    return row["price"] > 100 and row["region"] == "west"
mask = df.apply(check, axis=1)  # slow, loops in Python row by row

blocks.alt: Vectorized Boolean Logic on Full Columns
blocks.caption: The exact same logical result, computed the slow way instead of the fast way already available.

blocks.text: 6. iterrows and itertuples: The Slowest Options

iterrows() and itertuples() both let you loop over a DataFrame's rows in plain Python. They are explicitly named here because they are, genuinely, the slowest ways to touch a DataFrame's data that exist in pandas, row by row, in a real Python loop, with none of the vectorized machinery involved at all.

blocks.alt: iterrows and itertuples: The Slowest Options
blocks.caption: If you find yourself reaching for iterrows, stop and ask whether a vectorized alternative exists first, because it almost always does.

code.content:
# avoid this
for index, row in df.iterrows():
    df.loc[index, "total"] = row["price"] * row["quantity"]

# do this instead
df["total"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]

blocks.alt: iterrows and itertuples: The Slowest Options
blocks.caption: A real improvement over iterrows when a loop is truly unavoidable, but still nowhere close to vectorized speed.

blocks.title: If a loop truly seems unavoidable, use itertuples over iterrows
blocks.content: itertuples() returns lightweight named tuples instead of full Series objects per row, which is meaningfully faster than iterrows(). But before reaching for either one, spend a moment checking whether the operation can be expressed with np.where, np.select, boolean masking, or the .str accessor instead, since a genuinely vectorized rewrite is almost always available.

blocks.alt: iterrows and itertuples: The Slowest Options
blocks.caption: A rough mental ladder worth keeping in mind whenever you write a new pandas operation.

blocks.text: Say you need to assign each customer a risk tier based on a few threshold conditions across a couple of columns. Here is the slow, row wise version most people reach for first.
Here is the exact same logic, rewritten as a fully vectorized np.select call.

code.content:
conditions = [
    (df["credit_score"] < 580) & (df["late_payments"] > 3),
    df["credit_score"] < 670,
]
choices = ["high", "medium"]
df["risk"] = np.select(conditions, choices, default="low")

blocks.caption: Same result, same logic, dramatically less work under the hood on a large DataFrame.

blocks.text: On a large DataFrame, this kind of rewrite genuinely tends to run an order of magnitude faster, not a marginal improvement. The exact multiplier depends on your data and machine, but the general direction holds up consistently: fully vectorized code beats row wise apply by a wide margin every time the data gets big enough to matter.

items: pandas Series are backed by NumPy arrays, so the same vectorization speedup you learned in the NumPy module applies directly here.
np.where replaces a simple if/else apply, np.select replaces a whole if/elif chain.
The .str accessor is already vectorized, never loop over text with a plain Python string method.
Combine conditions with & and | directly on columns instead of writing a custom row wise comparison function.
iterrows is the slowest way to touch a DataFrame, itertuples is faster but still far behind vectorized code.
The general hierarchy, slowest to fastest: iterrows, itertuples, apply, fully vectorized.
